entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Gaius Antius Aulus Julius Quadratus was a Roman senator from Pergamon, who was appointed consul twice, in AD 94 and then in AD 105, the first senator from the Eastern Mediterranean to achieve the ordinary consulship. As a prominent figure in the Roman Senate, he played a crucial role in shaping the politics of the Eastern Roman Empire. His appointment as consul marked a significant milestone in the career of a senator from the provinces, highlighting the growing influence of the Eastern Mediterranean region in Roman politics. Quadratus' legacy can be seen in the continued importance of the Eastern Roman Empire in shaping the course of Western history. The Pergamene Senate, which Quadratus represented, was a hub of intellectual and cultural activity, fostering the development of Stoic philosophy and the arts. Despite the passing of centuries, the legacy of Gaius Antius Aulus Julius Quadratus continues to be felt in the contemporary world, where the principles of Stoicism remain influential in Western thought. The appointment of Quadratus as consul in AD 105 served as a testament to the growing power and influence of the Eastern Mediterranean region, a phenomenon that would have far-reaching consequences for the development of Western civilization. The Pergamene Senate, where Quadratus served, was a major center of learning and intellectual inquiry, attracting scholars and philosophers from across the ancient world. Quadratus' appointment as consul in AD 105 marked a significant moment in the history of the Eastern Roman Empire, one that would have lasting impacts on the development of Western politics and culture.
